title: Henrietta Swan Leavitt: The Yardstick of the Stars
source_book: Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (Harvard College Observatory Circular 173)
source_author: Henrietta Swan Leavitt & Edward C. Pickering
source_chapter: Harvard College Observatory Circular, Vol. 173, pp. 1-3
authenticity_note: Directly derived from Henrietta Swan Leavitt's 1908 and 1912 publications establishing the period-luminosity relationship of Cepheid variables, which allowed astronomers to measure the size of the cosmos.
summary: Working as a poorly paid human 'computer' at the Harvard Observatory, deaf astronomer Henrietta Swan Leavitt cataloged thousands of variable stars on glass plates. She discovered that brighter pulsing Cepheids took longer to pulse—giving astronomers the first universal standard candle to measure cosmic distances.
content:
In the early 1900s, Harvard College Observatory director Edward Pickering hired a group of talented women to analyze thousands of photographic glass plates of the night sky. Derisively called 'Pickering's Harem' and paid just 25 to 30 cents an hour, these women performed complex mathematical computations that male astronomers avoided.

Among them was Henrietta Swan Leavitt, a quiet, intensely focused scholar who had lost most of her hearing in her twenties. Henrietta was assigned the task of cataloging variable stars—stars whose brightness waxed and waned over days or weeks.

Armed with a magnifying glass, a millimeter ruler, and a notebook, Henrietta inspected the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dense star cluster visible from the Southern Hemisphere. Because all the stars in this distant cluster were roughly at the same distance from Earth, Henrietta realized that any difference in their apparent brightness on her plates reflected a real difference in their intrinsic luminosity.

By 1912, after painstakingly analyzing 1,777 variable stars, she discovered a stunning mathematical regularity: "A straight line can be readily drawn among each of the two series of points... the brighter variables have longer periods."

A Cepheid star that pulsed slowly was an inherently colossal beacon, while a rapid pulser was much dimmer! By simply clocking the pulse of a star with a stopwatch and photographic plates, astronomers could instantly know its true wattage ($L$). Comparing this true brightness to how faint it appeared from Earth immediately yielded its exact distance through the inverse-square law of light!

Henrietta Leavitt had handed humanity the first celestial yardstick. Without her discovery, Edwin Hubble could never have measured the distance to Andromeda or discovered the expanding universe. Though her name went largely unrecognized during her lifetime, today she is revered as one of the towering pioneers of modern cosmology.
